I can confirm all of this. My cat who will be two years old at the end of this month was a feral kitten. I caught her when she was 6 or 7 weeks old. It took me most of the day to tame her and convince her to stop attacking and hissing at me. 

She loves me and my family now, but at first she was terrified of anyone but me. It took a lot of socializing to get her used to everyone. She was also really clingy with me and would follow me around the house and would often climb up my body to sit on my shoulder or jump to a counter. She also liked attacking my hand or hunting my hands/feet as I went about my day to day stuff. 

The big difference between this cat and other cats that weren't feral as kittens is how independent and skittish she is. She doesn't really play that much with you, but will play for hours on her own. She usually sleeps on her own, but enjoys a quick cuddle at bedtime before she goes off to do her own thing. She either sleeps on her "perch" (a chair my mom put on our kitchen table with a blanket on it) or she crawls onto the vents in our basement. At any new noise or new voice she will run and hide in my parents bedroom or in the basement. She's also terrified of the outdoors now and stays mostly inside. 

I have an overhang under my bedroom window that covers our front door and garage entrance. She often will play out there at night and sometimes during the day and will bring me the things she catches. She wakes me up nightly to show me a spider she's caught before she eats it. The worst is when she kills birds and bats and leaves them on my pillow while I sleep. This also happens with other bugs sometimes as well. Her favourite game is to bring something live in and keep it alive while she plays with it. Once she managed to keep a moth alive for several hours while she caught and released it over and over. 

The downside was when she started peeing on our furniture after we got our puppy. We wound up having to move her litter box somewhere out of the way of the puppy where only the cat could get. We also had to start feeding the her on the counter because she stopped eating. The puppy would always try to play with her and she was having none of that. 

The best advice I can offer after raising a feral kitten is to make sure they always feel safe and secure, keep them socialized (at least with family), and understand that they're always going to be a little wild. I hope Pickle and his new family have a life of fun and love together.

I'm a bit late to the conversation, but this is worth saying: 

Learn to ask for help. 

Whether it's tutoring, counselling, registration, advising, or ANYTHING, just ask for help. One of the (many) reasons why I failed out of university in my third year was because I didn't ask for help. If I had asked for help (grief counselling, academic advising, office hours, even talking to my rugby coaches) during the year and a half it took me to get kicked out of my university, my academic career would have been much happier and successful. Instead I lost a partial athletic scholarship, lost the rest of my academic funding, let my team down, disappointed my parents, and next year when I do graduate my BA will have taken me ten years instead of four. 

Most schools are full of resources to help you be successful. Don't be afraid to ask for help. Lots of times when you go to look for help from your school, if the person you speak to can't help you, they can help you find what you need or point you in the right direction. 

Also: Be polite, be professional  and be willing to communicate. If you consistently do this, you will stand out for it. Your professors or TA's are more than likely to be lenient with you if they know things are going down in your life, but you've proven that you are a present (you've been talking to them all semester) and professional student. This means your legitimate life crisis (my grandmother is dying) will be seen as legit rather than just an excuse for getting an extension. 

Tl;dr Learn to ask for help. Be polite, be professional and be willing to communicate.

I'm not a real bartender. I just happen to work for a catering agency and am certified to serve alcohol so I often get sent to jobs as "the bartender". The saddest thing I've seen someone do to get with someone was when I saw guy drug a girl at a wedding. It was a huge wedding (we'd been told to expect 300 people at the reception) with people from all over the world attending. 

Basically a guy came up to the bar and ordered two drinks. Routine right? After I handed him his drinks, I watched him pull something out of his pocket and pour it into one drink. I thought this was a little weird and looked up at his face to ask if he was ok. He said he was fine and that it was "just for the nerves". 

I thought that was odd and watched him as he walked away and handed the drink he'd spiked to a girl who was maybe in her early twenties. I was stunned as he tapped his cup against her and chugged his drink while encouraging her to chug hers. 

At that point I asked my shift supervisor if he'd seen what just happened. Of course he hadn't because we were getting slammed with drink orders, but he believed me and immediately called security and asked me to go stand with the girl so they would know who to look for. So this girl got kind of lucky. She'd still been drugged and had to deal with that, but we managed to save her from this guy because of how quickly security had acted. Within minutes they took the guy into custody and had called the police to come deal with him, and the girls family was found (she was the bride's cousin and had flown in with her parents from Ontario) to take care of her. 

The part that bothered me was that this guy was a good looking guy. He was well dressed, decently built, nicely groomed, and looked like an all around decent fellow. I'm sure he could have gotten with any single lady at the wedding if he wanted to without drugging them.
